# The Founding of Hashomer Hatzair in Łuków.

## A youth movement enters Łuków

According to the memorial-book record, the **Founding of Hashomer Hatzair in Lukow** took place in **1925**, when three young people decided to establish a local branch of the movement. The record is attributed to [M. Bornstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_817fb9c2f0b7395faabad9c2), whose name appears in the connected evidence as the narrator of the episode. The surviving quotation, preserved in Hebrew and affected by OCR spacing and duplication, reads:

> “החלטנ ו לים ד בלוקו ב א ת הארגו ן של השומ ר הצעיר”

The supplied summary renders this as the decision “to establish the organization of Hashomer Hatzair in Lukow.” The date should be treated as **approximately or conventionally 1925**, since the source notes that the year appears as a duplicated range in the OCR. The memorial book identifies the passage as coming from **scan 156, printed page 152**. It does not provide, in the supplied excerpt, a detailed account of the founding meeting, its location, or the precise sequence by which the first branch was organized.

The three young people associated with the decision are [Zisel Feldman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_4aa41600466ffe4e7432437d) and [Shmuel Lichter](/communities/lukow/records/mention_10ec6a9fdf2c3f9b248710f8), together with the narrator, [M. Bornstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_817fb9c2f0b7395faabad9c2). The record explicitly says that Feldman and Lichter helped decide to establish Hashomer Hatzair in Łuków, while Bornstein is presented as the person who narrated the founding. This is a reasonable reconstruction of the “three young people” mentioned in the summary, although the supplied evidence does not spell out the three names in one uninterrupted sentence. The initials of M. Bornstein also leave the narrator’s full identity uncertain.

## Łuków’s Jewish setting

The new organization emerged within a large, deeply rooted, but increasingly diverse Jewish community. The memorial book characterizes the [Lukow Jewish community](/communities/lukow/records/mention_66df5f1594ada7e5aaedd1fc) as composed of people who were healthy, industrious, honest, and somewhat conservative. That description should not be read as implying political uniformity. Rather, the evidence suggests a community in which established religious and social traditions coexisted with energetic new movements among the younger generation.

Łuków had been an organized Jewish settlement by the sixteenth century, and its Jewish population grew substantially during the nineteenth century. By 1897, Jews numbered 4,799 people, or approximately 55 percent of the town’s population. The community possessed synagogues, batei midrash, a mikveh, charitable institutions, schools, and other communal structures. These details are described in the broader historical account of the town’s Jews on the page [History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

By the early twentieth century, Łuków was therefore not merely a place where a youth group could be imported from elsewhere. It was a substantial Jewish center with its own religious leadership, educational institutions, political organizations, cultural associations, and networks of migration. The town’s Jewish life remained strongly religious: the memorial-book chapter “Łuków, a Religious City” describes public life as concentrated around synagogues and houses of worship, while another memoir emphasizes that most of the Jewish population continued to observe the traditional way of life. At the same time, the same memorial-book material records the rise of socialism, labor activism, Zionism, and Jewish youth movements. The coexistence of these tendencies is essential to understanding why the founding of Hashomer Hatzair could be both innovative and locally significant.

## From traditional society to ideological youth culture

The founding belonged to a wider transformation in Jewish life after the First World War. The memorial book describes “strong ideological storms” that shook the previous serenity of Łuków. Poverty, shortages, memories of imperial oppression, and the dislocation caused by war helped draw many young Jews toward socialist, left-wing, and nationalist-Zionist ideas. Some young people moved away from the world of the beit midrash and from the inherited religious patterns of their parents, devoting themselves instead to the idealism of the modern Jewish youth movements.

This did not mean that Łuków ceased to be religious. The evidence explicitly preserves both sides of the picture: the continued strength of Agudat Yisrael and Orthodox communal leadership, and the expansion of socialist and Zionist youth organizations. The memorial book records the presence of the Bund and its youth movement Tsukunft, Poale Zion, the General Zionists, Mizrachi and Bnei Akiva, as well as Hashomer Hatzair. In the interwar period, the town’s Jewish youth thus encountered a spectrum of competing visions: religious continuity, Jewish socialism, parliamentary politics, territorial or cultural nationalism, and pioneering settlement in Palestine.

The surrounding historical account similarly describes Łuków as a town in which Bundist, socialist, labor, and Zionist organizations all operated. It notes that Hashomer Hatzair organized lectures and Jewish youth activities, while other Jewish parties maintained their own educational, cultural, or athletic institutions. These developments are summarized in [History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

## What Hashomer Hatzair represented

Hashomer Hatzair was not simply a recreational club or a scouting association. It was a Jewish youth movement that combined scouting, collective education, socialism, and Zionism. The movement originated in Galicia through the convergence of the Zionist scouting group Hashomer and the ideological circle Ze’irei Zion, which studied Zionism, socialism, and Jewish history. Its educational program emphasized the formation of a new kind of Jewish youth: physically active, socially cooperative, politically conscious, and committed to the possibility of building a collective Jewish life in Palestine.

The general history of the movement describes its early ideology as Marxist-Zionist and its educational influences as including Zionist thinker Ber Borochov, German youth culture, scouting, and the Wandervogel tradition. Hashomer Hatzair linked the emancipation of Jewish youth with *aliyah* and life in kibbutzim. These characteristics are outlined in the article [Hashomer Hatzair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashomer_Hatzair). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashomer_Hatzair)) The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum likewise defines Hashomer Hatzair as a Zionist-socialist pioneering movement intended to educate Jewish youth for kibbutz life in the Land of Israel, emphasizing education, personal fulfillment, scouting, and collective preparation. See the USHMM glossary entry [Resistance in the Smaller Ghettos of Eastern Europe: Glossary](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/resistance-in-the-smaller-ghettos-of-eastern-europe-glossary). ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/resistance-in-the-smaller-ghettos-of-eastern-europe-glossary))

For young people in Łuków, establishing a branch in 1925 would therefore have meant creating a framework for much more than political discussion. It could provide a social world of its own: meetings, study, outdoor activity, ceremonies, collective discipline, and an imagined future beyond the limitations of the town’s economy. The movement’s emphasis on preparation for pioneering life also offered a response to the restricted economic prospects confronting many Jewish young people in interwar Poland.

## The local branch and its activities

The memorial book’s broader account of Hashomer Hatzair in Łuków reveals the kind of organization that the 1925 initiative produced. It states that the movement gathered the majority of the town’s Jewish youth in its club and conducted cultural and educational programs within a Zionist environment. Its activities included lectures by speakers from Warsaw and a public Lag BaOmer march in blue-and-white uniforms. The description conveys both the movement’s local reach and its ability to turn ideology into visible communal culture.

The chapter identifies [Shmuel Lichter](/communities/lukow/records/mention_10ec6a9fdf2c3f9b248710f8) as one of the figures connected with the founding decision, while the wider account names Hersh Leib and Leah Lichter, Shmuel Huberman, and others as later leaders of Hashomer Hatzair in Łuków. The relationship between Shmuel Lichter in the founding record and the later references to the Lichter family or leadership circle is not fully clarified by the supplied evidence. It is therefore safest to say that the records place the Lichter name at the center of the movement’s early history, without asserting a specific family relationship that the excerpt does not document.

The movement’s activities were also shaped by the broader educational culture of Jewish Łuków. A memorial-book account recalls that members of Hashomer Hatzair met late into the night, that older or more experienced members prepared work for younger participants, and that groups sometimes went on night excursions to nearby towns or into the forest. There they pitched makeshift tents and listened to talks about kibbutz life and the dedication of pioneers and guards. This description suggests a movement that cultivated a deliberately alternative form of Jewish upbringing—one based on comradeship, physical activity, collective responsibility, and preparation for a pioneering future.

The JewishGen transcription of the relevant memorial-book pages records these activities, including the club’s cultural-educational work, Warsaw lectures, the Lag BaOmer procession, night trips, forest camps, and discussions of kibbutz life. See [Lukow, Poland: Pages 70–82, 88–91](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html). ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html))

## The role of the participants

The evidence gives only brief biographies of the people involved, but their roles are meaningful. [M. Bornstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_817fb9c2f0b7395faabad9c2) is important because the founding survives through his or her recollection. The account is therefore not an administrative record produced at the time, but a later act of communal remembrance. That perspective may explain why the event is remembered through a compact scene—the decision of three young people—rather than through membership lists, minutes, or a formal institutional chronology.

[Zisel Feldman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_4aa41600466ffe4e7432437d) appears as one of the young people who helped make the decision. The surname Feldman also appears in other Łuków memorial-book contexts, including references to Motel Feldman and to members of the town’s cultural and political life, but the supplied material does not establish that Zisel Feldman belonged to that particular family. It would be inappropriate to infer such a relationship solely from the shared surname.

[Shmuel Lichter](/communities/lukow/records/mention_10ec6a9fdf2c3f9b248710f8), whose record includes the honorific *z”l*—“of blessed memory”—is likewise remembered as a participant in the decision to establish the branch. The memorial book’s later account of Hashomer Hatzair mentions Lichter-named leaders, reinforcing the impression that the Lichter family or network was closely associated with the movement, although the available passage does not provide enough genealogical information to identify the precise connection.

A fourth figure, [Israel Rosenzweig](/communities/lukow/records/mention_915cc677f0ae06c00464680d), is described as a government-school teacher in Łuków and as a prospective youth leader. His presence points to an important institutional question: a youth movement needed not only enthusiastic founders but also adult educators, mentors, and links to the town’s educational world. The supplied record does not say that Rosenzweig formally directed the branch or that he was present at the founding decision. It does, however, place him within the movement’s expected leadership environment, suggesting that the young founders’ initiative was likely connected to a wider effort to provide Jewish youth with organized instruction and guidance.

## A movement within a crowded communal landscape

Hashomer Hatzair’s success in Łuków should also be understood in relation to the competition and dialogue among Jewish organizations. The memorial book says that the movement attracted a majority of the town’s Jewish youth, but it also records the strength of Agudat Yisrael, the activity of its youth federation, Bnei Akiva, the Bund and Tsukunft, Poale Zion, Beitar, and other organizations. Łuków’s young people were not choosing between “religion” and “nothing”; they were entering a crowded world of Jewish institutions, each offering a different interpretation of Jewish identity and the future.

The Orthodox camp remained powerful in the town. The JewishGen memorial-book material describes Agudat Yisrael as the largest faction in the Jewish community for much of the interwar period, with its own youth federation of young men and yeshiva students. At the same time, the same pages describe Jewish cultural and political activity as extending across libraries, schools, clubs, lectures, debates, sports associations, and youth groups. See [Lukow, Poland: Pages 70–82, 88–91](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html). ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/luk070.html))

In this setting, the founding of Hashomer Hatzair was an act of generational self-definition. The young founders were not merely adopting a foreign political label. They were creating a local institution through which Jewish youth could socialize, study, march, camp, debate, and imagine a collective future. The importance of the event lies precisely in this combination of local initiative and international ideology: three young people in Łuków translated a broad Jewish youth movement into an organization rooted in their own town.

## From interwar idealism to Holocaust remembrance

The later history of Hashomer Hatzair gives the 1925 founding an especially grave retrospective significance. Across occupied Poland, Jewish youth movements that had originally emphasized education, social transformation, and preparation for life in Palestine increasingly became centers of underground organization, mutual responsibility, and resistance. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes how Zionist youth leaders in wartime Poland assumed broader responsibilities, organized underground education, maintained communications between ghettos, and in some cases became leaders of armed resistance. This wider wartime context is discussed in [Jewish Youth Movements in Wartime Poland: From Minority to Leadership](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-youth-movements-in-wartime-poland-from-minority-to-leadership). ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-youth-movements-in-wartime-poland-from-minority-to-leadership?utm_source=openai))

The history of Łuków itself ended in catastrophe. German forces seized the town on **September 19, 1939**. During 1942 and 1943, Jews from Łuków and surrounding communities were deported to Treblinka, while many others were murdered in the town. The ghetto was finally liquidated on **May 2, 1943**. The account of Łuków’s Jewish history estimates that approximately 14,000 Jews from the Łuków ghetto and nearby towns and villages were sent to Treblinka, with approximately 2,000 more killed locally. These events are recorded in [History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w). ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

The memorial book was published in Tel Aviv in **1968** as *Sefer Lukow: gehelikt der khorev gevorener kehile*, translated as *The Book of Lukow: Dedicated to a Destroyed Community*. JewishGen describes it as a translation of the 652-page volume edited by B. Heller and published by former residents of Łuków in Israel and the United States. See [Łuków, Poland](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html). ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html)) The remembrance of the Hashomer Hatzair founding must therefore be read against the destruction of the society that produced it. What survives is not the branch’s complete membership register or institutional archive, but fragments of memory: a decision by three young people, a club filled with Jewish youth, blue-and-white uniforms, lectures, marches, forest excursions, and the hope of a different Jewish future.

## Significance of the 1925 founding

The founding of Hashomer Hatzair in Łuków marked the arrival—or more precisely, the local consolidation—of a new form of Jewish communal life. It joined the town’s longstanding religious and charitable institutions to a modern youth culture that was socialist, Zionist, educational, and collective. The initiative associated with [M. Bornstein](/communities/lukow/records/mention_817fb9c2f0b7395faabad9c2), [Zisel Feldman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_4aa41600466ffe4e7432437d), and [Shmuel Lichter](/communities/lukow/records/mention_10ec6a9fdf2c3f9b248710f8) was modest in form but far-reaching in implication.

The memorial book does not allow us to reconstruct every detail of the founding, and the date contains an OCR-related uncertainty. Nevertheless, the later descriptions of the branch make clear that this was not an isolated or short-lived experiment. Hashomer Hatzair became one of the principal institutions of Jewish youth in Łuków, combining cultural education with public ceremony, political idealism, outdoor activity, and preparation for pioneering life. In remembering its founding, the memorial book preserves a moment when Łuków’s young Jews sought to shape their own future—an aspiration that gives the event its historical importance and its enduring poignancy.
